questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The panic that exposed a gap in the law
questions.learningObjective: Explain the idea of a lender of last resort and the harm its absence caused.
questions.stem: Your group asks you to explain what a lender of last resort is and why the gap caused by its absence hurt.

answer.exemplar: A lender of last resort is an institution that will lend sound paper to a solvent bank that is temporarily short of cash, so that a panic does not spread from one frightened depositor to the next. In 1907 nothing filled that role federally, so a bank that was sound on its books could still fail for want of cash, and its failure deepened the fright that had caused the shortage in the first place.

questions.explanation: Without a lender of last resort, a sound bank could still fail for want of cash, and that failure deepened the panic. The gap is about who steps in with temporary money when a bank is squeezed.
questions.hint: Think about who lends to a bank that cannot borrow from its neighbours.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the national system was felt to be too thin
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a system bound by rules could not answer a crisis.
questions.stem: Explain why a system bound to pledged bonds and fixed reserve percentages could not answer a crisis.

answer.exemplar: Both rules tied money to something that could not move quickly. Notes could be issued only against bonds whose market value had fallen, so the supply of money shrank as the country grew, and a fixed reserve requirement meant a bank that paid out its balances lost lending power just as demand for credit was rising. In a run, neither rule could be the source of relief.

questions.explanation: Both rules tied money to something that could not move quickly, so the supply shrank when demand rose and banks lost lending power in a run. Neither rule could be a source of relief in a crisis.
questions.hint: Ask what each rule tied money to.

answer.exemplar: A rule-bound system tells institutions what to do, but it cannot tell them what to do next when everyone wants the same thing at once. questions.topic: What survived of a commission's plan
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the committee changed when it rewrote the commission's plan.
questions.stem: Because the outline notes that the plan was rewritten in committee, what changed in the rewrite?

options.text: The public character of the supervision was strengthened and private ownership of the reserve banks was dropped.
The regional structure was abandoned in favour of a single reserve bank in the capital.
options.misconception: Misses the change in the ownership proposal

options.text: The power to discount commercial paper was removed, because the committee distrusted banks.
options.misconception: Claims the discount power was dropped

options.text: The plan was withdrawn, and the statute was drafted from scratch without reference to it.
options.misconception: Turns a rewrite into a replacement

questions.explanation: The committee kept the plan's structure and made its supervision more public, dropping the proposal for private control of the reserve banks. A single bank, a lost discount power, and a discarded plan each misread it.
questions.hint: Look for the change in who would own and control the banks.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The clearing house rule that made a panic orderly
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the amount of clearing house certificates issued during the crisis.
questions.stem: A table of clearing house certificates issued during the crisis shows an amount. What does that amount show?

options.text: That the banks themselves, through their clearing house, provided temporary relief before any national facility existed.
That the federal government had already guaranteed the notes of the member banks.
options.misconception: Moves the guarantee to the federal government

options.text: That the certificates were issued in such volume that they became a permanent national currency.
options.misconception: Treats a temporary measure as a lasting currency

options.text: That the amount was raised by statute, since no private institution could have produced it.
options.misconception: Claims the amount came from legislation

questions.explanation: A large private issue of certificates shows the banks pooling their own resources to steady one another, which is why the crisis eased before a national system existed. A federal guarantee or lasting currency misread it.
questions.hint: Ask who issued the certificates behind that amount.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A statute that had to wait for a number
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a national lending facility was needed rather than private mutual help.
questions.stem: Explain why the country had to create a national facility with lending power rather than rely on the banks alone.

answer.exemplar: The banks could help one another only as far as their own resources and their own willingness went, and in the worst of the panic both were exhausted at once. A national facility with the power to lend against sound paper could put money into a solvent bank that was merely short of cash, at a moment when private confidence had collapsed, and that is a job no single bank could perform for itself.

questions.explanation: Private mutual help ran out exactly when it was most needed, since every bank was short at once, so a national lender had to put money in against sound paper. Leaving it to the banks cannot cover a run.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when every bank is short at the same time.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What survived of a commission's plan
questions.learningObjective: Identify which elements of the plan appeared in the final statute.
questions.stem: Which elements of the commission's plan appeared in the final statute?

options.text: Regional reserve banks, a central board of governors, membership for state banks, and the discounting of commercial paper.
A single reserve bank in the capital with no regional banks of any kind.
options.misconception: Adds a central bank that the statute did not create

options.text: A rule that only national banks could become members of the reserve banks.
options.misconception: Excludes the state bank membership the statute allowed

options.text: A prohibition on discounting any paper at the reserve banks in times of stress.
options.misconception: Invents a ban on discount lending

questions.explanation: The statute adopted the plan's regional banks, its board, its open membership, and its discount power, while changing the ownership question. A single bank, restricted membership, and a discount ban each misread it.
questions.hint: Check each element against the statute's structure.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The panic that exposed a gap in the law
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the events of the crisis as the session's slide presents them.
questions.stem: Sequence the events of the crisis as the session's slide lists them.

options.text: The corner, the bank's failure, the suspension of gold payments, the private agreement, then the new statute.
The corner, the suspension of gold payments, the bank's failure, the private agreement, then the new statute.
options.misconception: Swaps the failure and the suspension

options.text: The bank's failure, the corner, the private agreement, the suspension of gold payments, then the new statute.
options.misconception: Swaps the corner and the failure

options.text: The new statute, the corner, the bank's failure, the suspension, then the private agreement.
options.misconception: Places the statute at the front

questions.explanation: The slide runs from the failed corner through the bank's closure, the suspension of gold payments, the private agreement that restored settlement, and only then the statute. Every other order breaks the chain.
questions.hint: Keep the statute at the end of the chain.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A statute that had to wait for a number
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the central bank's own statutory reserve requirement.

stimulus.body: Each Federal reserve bank shall keep reserves in gold or silver, or other lawful money, equal to not less than forty per centum of its deposits, and shall keep reserves in eligible paper equal to not less than forty per centum of its deposits.

questions.stem: A quoted statute sets two reserve percentages for the central bank. What does the quoted rule show?

options.text: That the central bank itself was required to hold a substantial cushion of metal and of eligible paper against its deposits.
That the central bank was exempted from any reserve requirement because it was the lender of last resort.
options.misconception: Exempts the central bank from the quoted rule

options.text: That the quoted percentages applied to every bank in the country, including small country banks.
options.misconception: Extends the central bank's rule to all banks

options.text: That the central bank could lend without limit, since its own reserves were not counted against it.
options.misconception: Invents a carve-out for central bank lending

questions.explanation: The quoted rule makes the central bank subject to a substantial reserve cushion of its own, so it was not free to lend without limit. An exemption, a countrywide rule, and a lending carve-out each misread it.
questions.hint: Note which bank the rule binds.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The panic that exposed a gap in the law
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a banker's letter describing the crisis arrangement.

stimulus.body: We are convinced that the best service we can render the community is to keep the payments among ourselves moving, and we ask the association to stand behind us as we do so.

questions.stem: A banker's letter in the session packet describes the week's arrangement. What does it show?

options.text: That the leading bankers organized themselves to keep commerce running while the law stood still.
That the federal government ordered the clearing houses to lend to the weaker banks that week.
options.misconception: Turns a private agreement into a federal order

options.text: That the arrangement was already written into a statute before the crisis began.
options.misconception: Claims a statutory basis for the private agreement

options.text: That the members intended to abandon gold payments permanently in that city.
options.misconception: Reads a temporary measure as a permanent break

questions.explanation: The letter shows the bankers acting on their own initiative to keep payments moving while the law gave no answer, the situation the reform was written to end. A federal order or a permanent break each misread it.
questions.hint: Ask who is speaking and who is being asked to help.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order in which the silver question passed through Congress
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize what the reform settled and what it left open about silver.
questions.stem: Your group's synthesis asks what the reform settled and what it left open.

options.text: That the reform settled how money would be supplied in a crisis but left the silver question to the argument that had reopened it.
That the reform settled the silver question as well, so no dispute over money remained in the country.
options.misconception: Claims the reform ended the silver debate

options.text: That the reform settled nothing at all, because every provision it contained was replaced within a decade.
options.misconception: Claims total replacement of the statute

options.text: That the reform settled the currency question and reopened the silver question in the same act.
options.misconception: Invents a silver provision in the reform statute

questions.explanation: The reform answered the crisis and left the silver controversy standing, which is why the silver argument returned in later decades. A settled silver question, total replacement, and a silver provision each misread it.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two old questions was answered.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The panic that exposed a gap in the law
questions.learningObjective: Identify the specific gap at which the reform was aimed.
questions.stem: Read the crisis paragraph, then the reform paragraph, and state what the reform took aim at.

options.text: At the absence of any national power to expand the money supply and lend against sound paper when a run began.
At the silver question, which the reform resolved by setting a fixed ratio between the two metals.
options.misconception: Misidentifies the reform's target

options.text: At the state note tax, which the reform repealed along with the national note system.
options.misconception: Claims the reform repealed the note system

options.text: At the rule requiring national banks to deposit bonds, which the reform replaced with a fixed reserve percentage.
options.misconception: Says the reform ended the bond requirement

questions.explanation: The reform aimed at the gap the panic exposed, the absence of elastic currency and a lender of last resort, and that was the only question the crisis put on the table. Silver, the note tax, and the bond rule misidentify it.
questions.hint: Ask what the crisis showed the law could not do.
